newsitem.title: USA: Divided, puzzled Fed adopts cautious rate stance.
newsitem.headline: Divided, puzzled Fed adopts cautious rate stance.

text.p: Puzzled Federal Reserve policy-makers were divided at their May 20 meeting on whether to raise interest rates but ultimately decided to hold policy steady, minutes of the meeting released Thursday showed.

The vote in favour of steady policy was 9-1 with Richmond Fed President Alfred Broaddus dissenting in favour of higher rates to counter inflation. Some other policy-makers also argued for tighter credit but ultimately agreed to wait.

The policy-makers met again on Wednesday and again kept rates unchanged. The minutes of that meeting will not be released until late August, but the session was probably less contentious than in May because economic growth has clearly slowed since then.
The central bank raised short-term rates a quarter point on March 25 in a bid to keep the economy from overheating and inflation from rising.
At the May 20 meeting, Fed policy-makers also agreed that they might need to raise rates again "in the not too distant future" and unanimously voted to tilt policy in the direction.

The minutes showed that the policy-making members of the central bank's Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) were surprised and puzzled by the benign behaviour of inflation and were worried that it would not last, especially given the nation's tight job market that could lead to higher wages.

The labour market looks have to loosened a bit since that meeting. The government said Thursday the unemployment rate rose to 5 percent in June from a 24-year low of 4.8 percent in May. That sparked a surge in bond and stock prices as investors bet that the Fed will continue to hold off from raising rates.
At their May 20 meeting, FOMC members continued to voice concern about the risk of "some upturn" in inflation, "perhaps sooner rather than later."
The policy-makers also forecast that economic growth was likely to slow in the months ahead, but were nevertheless worried that such a slowdown might not contain inflation.
The economy grew at a 5.9 percent rate in the first quarter, its fastest pace in nine years. Growth in the second quarter probably slowed to about a 2 percent rate, economists said.
The FOMC members arguing for steady rates on May 20 pointed to slowing growth and the absence of higher inflation as justification for a cautious policy stance.
But they nevertheless "agreed that some (credit) tightening might well be needed later to contain potentially rising inflation," the minutes said.

Other FOMC members who preferred higher rates in the near term argued that a small rate rise would offer little risk of thwarting the six-year-old economic expansion but might head off the threat of higher inflation.

Broaddus dissented from the majority, arguing that strong investment demand risked spurring inflation and that the Fed needed to raise rates now to counteract that. All the FOMC members, though, agreed the inflation outlook was uncertain.
For months, the unemployment rate has been at levels that in the past have led to stepped-up wage demands and higher inflation. But that has not occurred.
"Recent developments had underscored the fact that historical experience was not a fully relieable guide to the prospective behaviour of prices," was the way the minutes of the May 20 meeting put it.

The policy-makers said faster-than-reported growth of worker productivity might be one reason that is the case. If workers are turning out more products, companies can afford to pay higher wages without cutting into their profits.
